1.d4 d5 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.cxd.strategy: Resolves the tension in the centre and forces Black to decide how to recapture. White gains the freer position, and each recapture leads to a different pawn structure and plan.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.cxd.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Semi-Tarrasch Defence

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the light-squared bishop, keeping the tension in the centre instead of exchanging on d5. White keeps the position solid and flexible, but resolves nothing: Black decides the pawn structure by how it reacts.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.Bg5.strategy: Pins the f6 knight to the queen, so the main defender of d5 cannot move freely. White adds pressure on the centre with a piece, and Black has to deal with the pin before the central tension can be released.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.e3.strategy: The normal reply: Black develops, adds a second attacker on d4 and keeps the position symmetrical. White now has to decide how to handle the centre: give Black an isolated pawn, accept one, or keep the symmetry and play with the extra tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.cxd.strategy: Retakes with the knight, the idea of the whole set-up: Black avoids an isolated pawn and puts a piece in the centre. The knight can be challenged by White's pieces and pawns, and in return for the free development Black accepts a space disadvantage.
Takes on d4 at once and opens the position for an early exchange of queens. Black accepts a fairly drawish game, and in the main line an endgame with doubled isolated pawns.

Retakes with the e-pawn and accepts the isolated d5 pawn of a Tarrasch structure, but with the knight already committed on f6 Black has less freedom than in that opening. The bishop on g5 can pin the knight, so this is a rarer and less comfortable choice.
